reasoning: ay becomes ee in urban speech (3eeno). ض is emphatic D, and ق is a glottal stop, so Dayyi'a. The idiom means stingy or tight-fisted, and is also heard as greedy.
The everyday Ramallah verb for 'got married' is itjawwaz. tzawwaj is the formal/MSA form. The English 'married' here means 'got married' (he-form).
Vulgar slang intensifier placed after an adjective (e.g. 7ilu fashakh). The meaning is right, but learners should know it is crude and not for polite company.
Hollow verb baan with b- prefix gives bibiin, with a long ii. ma negates the verb, and 3alayk becomes 3aleek. Used for things like 'you don't look your age'.
Urban Palestinian turns ث into t in native words (like تالت for ثالث), and ق is a glottal stop. So ti'iil, not thaqiil.
MSA-origin noun that is genuinely used. It belongs to the everyday root of 'addar (to appreciate), so ق is a glottal stop. It also means a grade or rating in school.
Standard Palestinian jisr with short i, with ج as j.

Country-name loanword. The vowel lengths are uncertain, since speakers vary between a long vowel and a shortened one. The scheme has no short o, so I wrote long vowels following the spelling. The English should be capitalised.
Taa marbuta after ح is e, giving naa7ye. Literally 'from one side', and usually paired with 'min naa7ye thaanye' (on the other hand).
Denominal verb from farshaayye (brush), as in farsha snaanu (he brushed his teeth). Alif maqsura is a. It is not the same as farrash (spread out, furnish).
il- stays il- before ب and م, which are moon letters, so il-ba7r and il-mayyit. mayyit is written with a doubled y.
ق is a glottal stop. In this construct phrase the taa marbuta becomes -it, so nu'Tit Da3f (nu'Ta on its own).
Masculine-addressee form, with the imperfect tiSba7 (ص emphatic) and ay becoming ee in kheer. Standard Palestinian good-night wish.
ث becomes t as in تالت. Palestinian taani is used more often as 'other / another / else' than as the ordinal 'second'.
Common Levantine idiom meaning secretly or behind the scenes. ح is 7, and the second ta7t carries the attached la- prefix.
ث becomes t and ق is a glottal stop. For an annoying person, ti'iil (or ti'iil id-damm) is the usual Palestinian usage.
Everyday word dunya. It also covers 'life' and 'the weather' (id-dunya bard).
Standard word for a grade average or GPA in Palestinian schools and universities. The د is doubled.
Colloquial verb for ignoring someone or something. ط is emphatic T and the ن is doubled. Very common in Palestinian speech too.
The spelling قرأ is MSA, but the spoken verb is 'ara, with a glottal stop for ق and no final hamza. Imperfect is bi'ra.
ma7taaj has a long aa, and ج is j. Taa marbuta after ي is e, giving 3amaliyye. The subject is implied.
Palestinian ween (not MSA ayna) plus ma kaan, meaning 'wherever it/he is'.
Palestinian miknase, with taa marbuta as e after س. It means a broom and is also used for a vacuum cleaner.
MSA-origin word that Palestinians genuinely use. Final hamza is written '. 'Identity' is more precisely huwiyye.
Blessing to a man, literally 'may God open it in your face'. Palestinian wijh has a short i, and the b- prefix attaches to it.
